latin: Mārcus Tullius Cicerō Titō Pompōniō Atticō S.P.D. (salūtem plūrimam dīcit).
Epistulam cum ā tē avidē exspectārem<sup>1</sup> ad vesperum, ut soleō, ecce nūntius puerōs vēnisse Rōmā.
Vocō, quaerō ecquid<sup>2</sup> litterārum. Negant.
«Quid ais, inquam, nihilne ā Pompōniō<sup>3</sup>?»
Perterritī vōce et vultū, cōnfessī sunt<sup>4</sup> sē accēpisse, sed excidisse<sup>5</sup> in viā.
Quid quaeris? Permolestē tulī: nūlla enim abs tē per hōs diēs epistula inānis aliquā rē ūtilī et suāvī vēnerat<sup>6</sup>.
Nunc sī quid in eā epistulā quam ante diem XVI Kalendās<sup>7</sup> maiās (ī.ē. diē 16° mēnsis Aprīlis) dedistī fuit historia dignum<sup>8</sup> scrībe quam prīmum nē<sup>9</sup> ignōrēmus.
Sīn<sup>10</sup> nihil praeter jocātiōnem, redde id ipsum!...
Sed cognōsce itinera nostra, ut statuās ubi nōs vīsūrus sīs<sup>11</sup>.

In Formiānum<sup>12</sup> volumus* venīre Parilibus<sup>13</sup>; inde Kalendīs Majīs (= diē 1° mēnsis Majī) dē Formiānō proficīscēmur ut Antiī<sup>14</sup> sīmus ā. d. V (ante diem quīntum) Nōnās Majās. (= 3° diē mēnsis Majī).
Lūdī enim Antiī futūrī sunt. Ēos Tullia<sup>15</sup> spectāre vult*.
Inde cōgitō in Tusculānum, deinde Arpīnum, Rōmam ad Kal. Juniās (= 1° diē mēnsis Jūniī).
Tē aut in Formiānō, aut Antiī, aut in Tusculānō cūrā ut videāmus.
Epistulam superiōrem restitue nōbīs et adpinge<sup>16</sup> aliquid nōvī.
Scrībēbam Antiī ā.d. XV Kal. Maī. annō 695° Ā.Ū.C. (ab Urbe conditā) (= 17/4/59 ante J.-C. nātum).
latinAccented: Mārcus Túllius Cícerō Titō Pompṓniō Átticō S.P.D. (salū́tem plū́rimam dīcit).
Epístulam cum ā tē ávidē exspectā́rem<sup>1</sup> ad vésperum, ut sóleō, ecce nū́ntius púerōs vēnísse Rōmā.
Vocō, quaerō ecquid<sup>2</sup> litterā́rum. Negant.
«Quid ais, inquam, nihílne ā Pompṓniō<sup>3</sup>?»
Pertérritī vōce et vultū, cōnféssī sunt<sup>4</sup> sē accēpísse, sed excidísse<sup>5</sup> in viā.
Quid quaeris? Permoléstē tulī: nūlla enim abs tē per hōs diēs epístula inā́nis áliquā rē ū́tilī et suā́vī vḗnerat<sup>6</sup>.
Nunc sī quid in eā epístulā quam ante diem XVI Kaléndās<sup>7</sup> máiās (ī.ē. diē 16° mēnsis Aprī́lis) dedístī fuit história dignum<sup>8</sup> scrībe quam prīmum nē<sup>9</sup> ignōrḗmus.
Sīn<sup>10</sup> nihil praeter jocātiṓnem, redde id ipsum!...
Sed cognṓsce itínera nostra, ut státuās ubi nōs vīsū́rus sīs<sup>11</sup>.

In Formiā́num<sup>12</sup> vólumus* venī́re Parílibus<sup>13</sup>; inde Kaléndīs Majīs (= diē 1° mēnsis Majī) dē Formiā́nō proficīscḗmur ut Ántiī<sup>14</sup> sīmus ā. d. V (ante diem quīntum) Nōnās Majās. (= 3° diē mēnsis Majī).
Lūdī enim Ántiī futū́rī sunt. Ēos Túllia<sup>15</sup> spectā́re vult*.
Inde cṓgitō in Tusculā́num, deínde Arpī́num, Rōmam ad Kal. Júniās (= 1° diē mēnsis Jū́niī).
Tē aut in Formiā́nō, aut Ántiī, aut in Tusculā́nō cūrā ut videā́mus.
Epístulam superiṓrem restítue nōbīs et adpínge<sup>16</sup> áliquid nōvī.
Scrībḗbam Ántiī ā.d. XV Kal. Maī. annō 695° Ā.Ū.C. (ab Urbe cónditā) (= 17/4/59 ante J.-C. nātum).
english: M. T. Cicero [sends his best greetings] (gives very much greeting) to Titus Pomponius Atticus.
As I was impatiently awaiting a letter from you towards evening, as [is my] habit, here is the news that two [boys] have arrived from Rome.
I call them, I ask [whether they have a letter] (is it that anything of letters). [They answer that they have not] (they deny).
«What are you saying, I exclaimed, nothing from Pomponius?»
Completely terrified by [my] voice and [my] attitude (face), they confessed that they had received [one] but that it had fallen on the road.
[What do you want]! (you seek) I took [it] very badly: indeed all these days I have not received from you any letter [which did not contain something] (empty of) useful and agreeable.
Now, if in this letter that [you sent] (gave) on 16 April there was something worthy of interest (history), write as soon as possible so that we [do not remain] ignorant [of it].
If [it contains] nothing [other than] (except) banter, send it to me [too] (that very thing)!...
But you [must] know our itinerary(ies) so that you may decide where you will [come to] see us.
We want to arrive at [our property at] Formiae, for the Parilia (see note); [then, from there], on 1 May, we will leave Formiae [so as to be] at Antium on 3 May.
There must in fact be games at Antium. Tullia wants to see them.
From there I think [to go] to [my property at Tusculum] (the Tusculan), then to Arpinum, [and] to Rome for 1 June.
Make sure (cura) that we [see you] either at Formiae, or at Antium, or at Tusculum.
[Send us back] your previous letter and add something new (see note 16).
[Done] (I was writing) at Antium on 17 April, etc.

footnotes: Cum, temporal, calls for the subjunctive (exspectarem, subj. impf.) if the tense of the subordinate is in the imperfect or the pluperfect.
Ecquis, ecqua (or ecquae), ecquid, interrogative pronoun, is there someone who...?, is there something...?

Pomponio: It is evidently a question of Titus Pomponius Atticus, a former schoolmate with whom Cicero exchanged an abundant correspondence. We remind you: Titus, first name; Pomponius, family name (of the gens Pomponia) and Atticus, the Athenian, nickname which was the consequence of a long and fruitful stay in Athens. Cicero belonged to the gens Tullia and his cognomen comes from cicer, -eris, n., which we saw in L. 58, P. 4.
Confiteor, -eris, -eri, fessus sum (cum + fateor, to declare), to avow, to confess.
Excido, -is, -ere, cidi (ex + cado), to fall from, to slip from the hands.

P. 6, w. f. w.: No letter from (abs = ab) you empty of useful and agreeable thing had arrived; in other words, all your letters are interesting (two negations are worth an affirmation). Inanis, -e, empty; likewise utilis and suavis are adjectives of the 3rd declension (parisyllabic); inane, the void (physical).

Kalendae, -arum, f. pl.: the ancient Roman calendar, and even the Julian calendar (improved calendar by a reform of Julius Caesar in 46 B.C.) were rather complicated. Instead of counting the days from the beginning of the month, they were counted backwards from certain particular dates: the CALENDS (1st of the month), the NONES (nonae, 5th or 7th day of the month, but 9th day in the count backwards from the ides, whence their name), and the IDES (idus, abl. idibus, 13th or 15th of the month). For additional information, you can consult the classical grammar or any other specialized work.

Historia dignum: after adjectives such as dignus (worthy of), contentus (satisfied with), plenus (full of), and after their contraries, the ablative is used. E.g.: dignus verbere, worthy of the whip; contentus sorte sua, satisfied with his lot; vacuus petroleo, empty of petrol; see above inanis re utili. However, some of these same adjectives can be followed by the genitive: plenus vini, full of wine.
Sin = si + negation, if on the contrary.
Statuo, -is, -ere, -ui, -utum, to fix; same root as stare. Visurus sis: future participle + present subjunctive of esse = future subjunctive.

Formianus, -a, -um, of Formiae (Formiae, -arum, f. pl.), town where Cicero had a property. Likewise Tusculanum, adj., designates here another property situated at Tusculum. From which it follows that M. Cicero was not among the economically weak!
Parilia, -ium, pl. n. (or Palilia): feasts in honour of Pales, goddess of flocks, which took place on 21 April.
Antium, -ii, n., Antium, in Italian Anzio.
Tullia: Cicero was called Marcus Tullius; the feminine proper name Tullia designates Cicero's daughter.
Adpingo, -is, -ere, pinxi, pictum, to add by painting (ad + pingere, same conjugation, to paint).
comments: N.B. — We remind you that this letter has been cut and retouched (address and date in particular). If you want to know the exact form of Cicero's correspondence you will have to refer to a classical edition (see BIBLIOGRAPHICAL INDEX, p. 546).
Proverb. — Ignarus redit Romam deductus asellus. — The donkey [that one has] led to Rome comes back [just as] ignorant (= he who goes to Rome a fool comes back one).

Gai, vocative of Gaius (or Caius, for the c and the g formerly made only one and the same letter, corresponding to the Greek gamma). — Pilicrepus, -i, m., pelota player (a game analogous to Basque pelota); pila, -ae, f., the ball; crepare, to crack. — Patruus, paternal uncle (father's brother, cf. L. 80); avunculus (cf. L. 30), which has given the French oncle, corresponds to the maternal uncle (mother's brother). — Quoties... toties, how many times... so many times, correlative adverbs of time.

latin: Gāī mīles! oppidum oppugnandō fortiter tē gessistī.
Commeātum 15 diērum habēbis. Quō adīre* vīs*?
Grātiās, Centuriō! Nemausum īre* cupiō.
Lūdōs enim quī Nemausī futūrī sunt libentissimē spectem.
Māvīs* gladiātōrum pugnās spectāre quam in hostēs ipse irruēre!
Tauromachīīs adesse* mālō*, vel etiam pilīcrepōrum lūdis.
Quae erit, commeātus tempore, īnscrīptiō tua?
Apud patruum erō, quī aedēs in forō frūmentāriō habet.
Quotiēscumque in difficultāte nummāriā sum, totiēs pecūniam mihi commodat.
Gāī mīles, nūlla est in tē gravitās; timeō nē commeātus iste pessimē succēdat.
latinAccented: Gāī mīles! óppidum oppugnándō fórtiter tē gessístī.
Commeā́tum 15 diḗrum habḗbis. Quō adī́re* vīs*?
Grā́tiās, Centúriō! Nemáusum īre* cúpiō.
Lūdōs enim quī Nemáusī futū́rī sunt libentíssimē spectem.
Māvīs* gladiātṓrum pugnās spectā́re quam in hostēs ipse irruḗre!
Tauromachī́īs adésse* mālō*, vel étiam pilīcrepṓrum lūdis.
Quae erit, commeā́tus témpore, īnscrī́ptiō tua?
Apud pátruum erō, quī aedēs in forō frūmentā́riō habet.
Quotiēscúmque in difficultā́te nummā́riā sum, tótiēs pecū́niam mihi cómmodat.
Gāī mīles, nūlla est in tē grávitās; tímeō nē commeā́tus iste péssimē succḗdat.
english: Soldier Gaius! You conducted yourself courageously [in the siege of] (besieging) the stronghold.
You will have a fifteen-day leave. Where do you want to go?
Thank you, [my] captain! I wish to go to Nîmes.
I would go very willingly [to see] the games that must take place in Nîmes (you would see).
You prefer to see gladiator fights rather than go yourself to the assault (in) of the enemies!
I prefer to attend [bullfights] (tauromachies) or even [Basque] pelota matches.
What will your address be during the time of [your] leave?
I will be with my paternal uncle, who has a house in the grain market.
Every time I am in financial difficulties, [as often] he lends me money.
Soldier Gaius, [you are not serious] (no seriousness is in you): I fear that this leave will turn out very badly.
